Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.raw: Sign language names, or name signs, work quite differently from spoken names. Usually you're given a name sign by your Deaf friends, and it's based on a salient physical feature, like big ears or a squint, or maybe a personality trait. Or it could be just a metaphorical connection, like if you like leopards, they might call you Leopard. And it's a very important part of Deaf culture that the name sign is given by your peer group, so you don't just give yourself a name sign. People tend to use the same name sign, so there's consistency across the Deaf community. And the name sign is used in the same way that you would use someone's name in English, just to refer to someone, to call their attention, to identify them, to talk about them in the third person. And it's just very common to use name signs.

items.raw: Sign language has its own way of making names. It's not just miming or signed fingerspelling. It's a name sign or a personal name, and that's a word that's usually based on some quality of the person, whether it's their appearance, their personality, something that happened to them. And it's really a very nice system because it's easy to reproduce and easy to understand, and it's not very long.

Question: why child support is based on income rather than what a child would need monthly.
items.raw: Child support formulas are a compromise of sorts. Ideally, we would do an expense model, like a budget, and say this child is going to need this much for food and clothes and childcare, and that's what we're going to charge. The problem is that it's very subjective. Parents disagree on what's necessary and what's extravagant. Income is a very objective number. You can go get tax returns, pay stubs, and everybody agrees on what the income is. So, it's a rough proxy for what the parents can afford to pay. That's why we use income. We look at the income of both parents and then we prorate that and give the noncustodial parent a percentage. So it's a percentage of their income, not of the child's needs. That's the best that we can do, and it's much more objective and predictable for the courts and for the parents.

Question: When popcorn is popping, what is actually happening to the kernel inside?
items.raw: I think about popcorn in a way not a lot of people do. I think about the thermodynamics of it. What's actually happening is that the kernel is this closed vessel. It's got a very thick, hard shell, the pericarp, that is impermeable to water. And so, when you heat it, the water inside the kernel turns to steam. And it can't escape, so it just builds up pressure. And the starch inside the kernel is also being gelatinized. It's going from a solid crystalline state to a more liquid, amorphous state. And so, as the pressure builds, the starch is getting softer and softer and more pliable. And the shell is rigid. And eventually, the pressure inside gets high enough that the shell just fails. It breaks. And when it breaks, the starch is still very hot. The water is still very hot. The pressure is coming down very rapidly. And so, it expands. It expands up to 30 or 40 times its original volume. And the starch just expands into this amorphous solid. It solidifies. It makes the popcorn. And if the popcorn is well popped, you have this very light, fluffy, solid material. And it's mostly air, like 90% air. And it's very light. And it's very crispy because the starch is very dry. It's very brittle. If you don't pop it well, if it's under pressure or if it's not hot enough, it doesn't fully expand. And it makes a very dense popcorn. It's very chewy. It's not very good. It's called a butterball. And if it's too hot, it burns, it turns to carbon. And so, you want to hit the sweet spot. The sweet spot is about 180 degrees Celsius, 350 degrees Fahrenheit. That's when you want to pop it. And the pressure inside at that point is about 130 pounds per square inch, which is a very high pressure. And so, it's a very violent failure. And the popcorn actually launches itself. It flies out. It pops out of the kettle. It's very dramatic. And it's a very interesting process.

Question: When popcorn is popping, what is actually happening to the kernel inside?
items.raw: I think there's a misconception that popcorn popping is just an explosion, like a little grenade. It's actually a very specific and beautiful thermodynamic process. So the popcorn kernel has this very dense starch, it's basically just starch inside, and it's very dense and solid, and then it's sealed inside this very tough, impermeable hull, that's the hard part of the kernel. So the starch is very, very sealed in. And when you heat it, the water inside the kernel, there's only a few percent water in the kernel, starts to boil, and it can't escape because it's sealed in. So it creates this tremendous pressure, several atmospheres of pressure, inside the kernel. And at some point, the starch actually melts and turns into this liquid, very fluid starch. And then the pressure is just too great, and the hull breaks. And when the hull breaks, all that pressure is released, and the water just flashes to steam. It goes from liquid to vapor instantly, and it expands to about 50 times its volume. And it takes the starch with it. So the starch just expands into this fluffy, foamy structure, and it's essentially foam. That's popcorn. It's foam. It's starch foam. And then as it cools down, it solidifies, and you get this very fluffy, light, airy structure. And it's just starch and water, and then maybe a little bit of protein and fiber. But it's really just starch and water that's been turned into this foam. So it's a really neat process. I like popcorn, I'm a fan of popcorn. But I think it's very underrated as a snack. It's very low calorie, it's very low fat, it's high in fiber, it's high in protein. It's very good for you, as long as you don't add all the butter and salt and sugar. So I think popcorn is a really underrated snack. It's very healthy, it's very good for you. It's got a lot of antioxidants in it. It's a whole grain, it's whole corn. So I think popcorn is a really underrated snack. And I think it's interesting to think about what's actually happening in there. It's really a very neat process, this thermodynamic process that's taking place inside the kernel.

Question: When popcorn is popping, what is actually happening to the kernel inside?
items.raw: I think the popcorn popping mechanism is really interesting. And I think we're best able to understand it with a little bit of physics. So we're talking about this little kernel of corn that's been dried out. It's just this very hard little shell. And inside that shell, there's a little bit of starch and a little bit of water. And that water, it's just trapped inside this shell. And it's a very, very hard shell. It's very thick and very tough. So it's really holding in that water. And when we start to heat it up, that water inside, it's going to start to turn into steam. And that steam is going to start to pressurize inside the little kernel. And the pressure will build and build and build. And it's going to eventually reach something like 135 pounds per square inch inside this little kernel. That's about 10 times the pressure of a car tire. And then eventually, that shell just can't hold it in anymore. It fails. And the pressure just explodes outward. And the steam, it's going to take the starch with it, and it's going to puff it up. And then it's going to expand and solidify and form this little popcorn puffy thing that we eat. So the whole thing is really just the pressure inside the little kernel. And then when it fails, it expands and it solidifies. And that's all there is to it. But I think it's really interesting that this shell is so strong. And I think it's really interesting that the popcorn expands about 40 times its original volume. And I think we can see that if we look at the inside of a popcorn, it's very porous. It's very puffy. And it's got a lot of little air pockets in it. And that's because it's just expanded so much. And the reason it doesn't just collapse back down and become a kernel again is because it solidifies. So it's very, very fragile. And if you take a popcorn and you just squeeze it, it'll break. It'll just fall apart. But if you just leave it alone, it'll stay puffed up forever. And that's why we love it. We love eating it. It's just very light and fluffy. And that's just the result of this pressure, this explosion, this expansion and solidification.

At 3:12 every Thursday morning, Mara found the book in the bread rack.

It was always the same one: The Practical Guide to Inland Birds, cracked blue spine, library stamp from a town forty miles away. She would set it on the flour bin, wipe butter from the cover, and mean to take it back after her shift. By noon, the errands and heat and sleep would swallow the thought.

Then, next Thursday, there it would be again, tucked between cooling rye loaves.

Tonight the bakery hummed with the proofing cabinet and the old radio’s static. Rain pressed silver lines down the front window. Mara lifted the book with both hands, as if it might be warm.

A folded receipt marked the chapter on herons.

She opened it.

In block letters, someone had written: I THINK YOU ARE THE ONLY PERSON AWAKE WHEN I AM. PAGE 47.

Mara turned to page 47. A grey heron stood in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint. Under the picture, in pencil: THURSDAY, 3:30?

The clock over the mixer clicked once.

Mara brushed flour from her apron, unlocked the front door, and turned on the little OPEN sign.

A simple rain gauge measures rainfall by catching precipitation in a funnel and directing it into a cylindrical measuring tube. 

To ensure accurate and easy reading, the gauge's top opening is deliberately wider than the inner measuring tube. This difference in diameter acts as an amplifier. For example, if the collection opening has ten times the area of the inner tube, one inch of rainfall will fill the tube to a height of ten inches. This magnification allows observers to easily and precisely read very small amounts of rainfall, such as hundredths of an inch.

However, these instruments are subject to errors. One common source of inaccuracy is evaporation; collected water can quickly evaporate before it is measured, especially in warm or windy weather. Another major source is wind exposure. Strong winds can create turbulence around the gauge's mouth, carrying raindrops over the opening and causing the instrument to underestimate the actual rainfall.

So if the top area is 10 times the area of the inner tube, then one inch of rain will fill the tube to 10 inches. Question: Why is the USA drinking age set at 21 when in most other respects you're an adult at 18.
items.raw: The drinking age in the United States at 21 is a somewhat strange legal convention that's actually very unusual in the global context. Most countries, like in Europe, set it at 18. Some even at 16. So it's an anomaly. And there's a very particular set of circumstances in the 1970s that resulted in it being set at 21. In the 1970s, there was a lot of discussion about lowering the voting age, because in the Vietnam War, you were being drafted at 18, and then you weren't allowed to vote. So there was a whole movement to lower the voting age to 18, and then the states started lowering the drinking age to 18, 19, and 20. And then there was a whole set of statistics that showed that young people between 18 and 20 were having a lot more car accidents, a lot more drunk driving accidents. And so Congress in 1984 passed a law that said that if a state didn't set its drinking age to 21, it would lose 10 percent of its federal highway funds. And because that was a very strong incentive, most of the states set the drinking age to 21. So it's really a function of drunk driving. It's not necessarily about health or maturity. It's just about the number of car accidents that were happening in the 1970s and 1980s. And there have been some studies now that say that maybe the drinking age of 21 isn't necessarily the optimal age to start drinking, that maybe 18 or 19 would be better. But it's very hard to actually lower that drinking age in the United States, because we have a very conservative political environment, and people like to think that young people should be more disciplined and not drink alcohol. So it's really a very political decision, not necessarily a scientific one.

And so the federal government came in and said, we're going to give you some highway money, but you have to raise the drinking age to 21. Question: What's the difference between tornadoes, hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons etc?
items.raw: These are all rotating weather systems driven by pressure differences and the Coriolis effect. The name we use for them mostly depends on where in the world they are, and how strong they are, and how big they are. So a cyclone is the general term for any rotating storm system. And then in the Atlantic, and in the eastern Pacific, we call them hurricanes. In the western Pacific, we call them typhoons. In the Indian Ocean, we call them cyclones. So it's really just geography, where the storm is. And then, tornadoes, they are a very different thing. Tornadoes are very small rotating columns of air that are a few hundred meters in diameter. They're very intense. They're very powerful, very strong winds. But they're small and short-lived. They only last for a few minutes to maybe 10 minutes, 15 minutes, rarely longer. They're usually associated with very strong thunderstorms, supercells. And they can form in the middle of the continent, they can form near the ocean, they can form anywhere. Hurricanes, typhoons, cyclones, they have to form over the ocean. They need water, they need warm water. They need to be over water to get the energy to sustain themselves. So they're different in that sense. And they're much bigger, they're a few hundred kilometers in diameter. And they can last for days, for a week, for two weeks, for three weeks. So they're much longer-lived, much bigger, but they're not as intense as tornadoes. A tornado can have winds of 200, 250, 300 miles per hour. A hurricane, the strongest ones, can be 150, 160, 170, 180 miles per hour. So tornadoes are more intense, but they're much smaller and much shorter-lived. And then, we have different scales for hurricanes and tornadoes. So for tornadoes, we have the EF scale, from EF0 to EF5. EF5 is the strongest, EF0 is the weakest. And for hurricanes, we have the Saffir-Simpson scale, from category 1 to category 5. Category 5 is the strongest, category 1 is the weakest. So we have these scales to quantify the intensity of these weather systems.

Question: After a recent deed, someone told "that was mighty white of ya". What does that phrase mean?
items.raw: I think people sometimes abuse the term "white of ya" or "white of you." I think it's meant to be sincere, or at least it's meant to be sincere. But I think it's used in a way that's very performative, very flattery, that can be really awkward for the person that's being complimented in that way. I think that, especially to me, the connotation of white is this benevolent, helpful, generous, self-sacrificing, maybe saintly, moral, pure person. And so, I think when you say, "That was really white of you," you're actually putting this person up on a very high pedestal. And I think that's a little bit uncomfortable for the person being complimented. I also think that it's really reductive and very surface level. So, I think a better compliment would be, "Thank you for what you did. I really appreciated it, and it really meant a lot to me," or "I really appreciate the time and energy that you spent doing that for me." And that's a lot more sincere, a lot more genuine, and a lot less performative. And I don't think you're putting the person on this pedestal where they're like, I'm a saint, I'm super moral, I'm super selfless, I'm super pure. And I think that's a little bit uncomfortable. I think it's a compliment that I get a lot, and I always feel a little weird, and I always want to take it off. I want to take the pedestal off and just say, "Yeah, you're welcome. I'm glad I could do it." And I think that's the sincere way to do it.

Postmodernism is not that everything is relative and it doesn't really matter and it's just your opinion. That's kind of a very straw man argument of what postmodernism is. Postmodernism is that we are really in a very fragmented world, and that there are many ways to see things, but that doesn't mean that everything is equally valid. And so, I think of it as the idea that there are these big totalizing narratives that tell us what is true. What is right? What is beautiful? What is moral? And postmodernism says, well, who decided that? Who's the one who's defining that truth, that beauty, that morality? And so, it's a very skeptical look at these big narratives that have been dominant in the West, that have been dominant in Europe for centuries, and saying, who's getting left out of these narratives? Who's not being counted in? What stories are we not telling? What's missing? And so, it's very much a liberating project, I think, of letting in all these different voices that have been left out. It doesn't say that we don't have truth. I think we do. But I think that truth is very much a cultural construct, that it's constructed, it's made by us. And so, we have to interrogate who's making it. And so, for example, in art, postmodern art is very much about breaking down the idea of what is high art and what is low art. It's the idea that a banana taped to the wall is art. And it's the idea that a collage, that's made out of a bunch of different magazine pages, is art. And it's breaking down these very rigid hierarchies of what is art. It's about mixing and matching different traditions, different genres, different styles. So, it's a very playful idea. It's very playful and very fun, and I think it's liberating. I think it's very much a celebration of difference and diversity. I don't think it's a very pessimistic project. I think people have just gotten it wrong. They've made it sound very pessimistic and very nihilistic. And I think that's really a mischaracterization. It's a very optimistic, playful, celebratory project that's just very much about asking, who's the one that's defining the rules, and maybe we can break the rules.

Question: Can someone explain Post-Modernism like I'm 5, please?
items.raw: I think postmodernism is basically the realization that the very prescriptive rules we used to rely on a lot to structure things are no longer functional. So, I think of it as the kid who goes to a religion school for 10 years and then suddenly becomes an atheist. And now they look back at all the things they believed, and they're like, "Who decided that that's true? Why is it true? Why do we believe it?" And they're questioning all of the authority. So in literature, postmodernism is this idea that the way we were writing stories, the heroic narrative, the protagonist, the antagonist, the journey, the hero's journey, that structure is no longer functional. And we can play with structure. We can play with structure and play with language and play with time and play with the perspective. So we're going to tell the story from a bunch of different points of view. We're going to play with time. We're going to break it up. We're going to go forward and backward. We're going to tell the story from the perspective of a dog. We're going to tell the story from the perspective of a tree. We're going to tell the story from the perspective of the villain. We're going to play with that. And we're going to question the authority of the author. Who said the author is in charge? And we're going to play with the language, with the words, the connotation of the words, the denotation of the words. We're going to play with how they're structured, how they're put together. And we're going to play with the metafiction, the idea that we're talking about a novel inside a novel, that we're talking about the act of writing a novel, and we're questioning the novel itself. So it's very playful, very self-aware. And I think that's where it's useful and where it's fun. But I do think it can be very alienating to readers because it can be very hard to follow, and it can be very confusing and very esoteric. And I think that's the downfall of postmodernism, that it became a very academic movement. And it became very, very difficult to read. And that's where I think it lost a lot of its power. And that's where I think it became less relevant to a lot of people. But I think that it's a really fun way to write, and it's a really fun way to play with the structure of a story and the structure of a novel. And I love it.

So you have the low frequencies at the center and the high frequencies at the outside. And then they just do some fancy graphics with it. So they make it look like a sun. And for the others, they just do different things. So it's really just the same underlying data, the frequency bands, just displayed in different ways.
